questions.q: How is Salesforce's 75% code coverage requirement calculated?
options: Per individual class only, with no org-wide requirement
Across the org's Apex code as a whole, so one poorly-tested large class can drag the average down
Only on triggers, not on regular Apex classes
As an average of each developer's personal coverage score
questions.explain: The 75% requirement is computed org-wide across all Apex code, not class by class — a single large, poorly-covered class can pull the overall average below the threshold.

questions.q: A class has 100% code coverage, but one trigger in the org has 0% coverage. Can the org deploy new Apex to production?
options: Yes, because the org-wide average is what matters, not any individual trigger
No — every trigger needs its own test coverage regardless of how well other classes are covered
Yes, as long as the trigger has no DML statements
No, but only if the trigger was written in the last 24 hours
questions.explain: Separately from the org-wide 75% average, every trigger must have some test coverage of its own — a 0%-covered trigger blocks deployment even if other classes are fully covered.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT count toward or against Apex code coverage calculations?
options: Lines inside a public service method
Lines inside a trigger handler
Calls to System.debug
Branches of an if/else statement in application code
questions.explain: System.debug calls never count toward code coverage, whether or not they execute; coverage is measured only against real application logic.

questions.q: In the calculateDiscount(amount, tier) example, a test only calls it with tier = 'Gold'. What does this leave unproven?
options: Nothing — calling the method once is sufficient to prove it correct
The behavior of the Silver branch and the fallback return 0 case remain unexercised and unproven
The method will fail to compile without testing every branch
Governor limits are automatically violated
questions.explain: Only testing the Gold branch leaves the Silver branch and the default fallback case completely unproven, even though the class might still show a reasonably high coverage percentage.

questions.q: Where in Setup can you check a class's most recent code coverage percentage?
options: The Profiles page
The Apex Classes page's '% Covered' column
The Object Manager
The Flow Builder canvas
questions.explain: Setup's Apex Classes page lists every class with a '% Covered' column reflecting the most recent test run.
